## The Disappearing Yeast: A Kitchen Chemistry Mystery

### 1. The Problem: Solid to Liquid Transformation

The experiment you described presents an intriguing puzzle: how can solid yeast and sugar seemingly dissolve into a liquid within minutes? To understand this phenomenon, let's break down the process step by step.

### 2. Step-by-Step Reasoning

**a) Yeast: A Living Organism:**

- Baker's yeast, unlike dry yeast, is a living organism composed of single-celled fungi called Saccharomyces cerevisiae. These cells have a semi-permeable membrane that allows the passage of certain molecules.

**b) Sugar: The Fuel Source:**

- Sugar, in this case, acts as a readily available food source for the yeast. When it comes into contact with the yeast cells, it triggers a series of chemical reactions.

**c) The Power of Osmosis:**

- The key to understanding the "disappearing" act lies in a process called osmosis. Due to the concentration difference, water from the surrounding environment (including the moisture within the yeast cells) moves across the semi-permeable membrane into the sugar solution. This influx of water causes the yeast cells to swell and eventually burst, releasing their internal contents.

**d) Enzymes and Chemical Reactions:**

- The released yeast enzymes, along with the dissolved sugar, participate in a series of biochemical reactions, primarily fermentation. During fermentation, the yeast breaks down the sugar molecules into simpler compounds, releasing carbon dioxide (CO2) as a byproduct.

**e) The Liquid Result:**

- The combination of the influx of water, the breakdown of sugar, and the release of CO2 results in a significant increase in the volume of the mixture. This, coupled with the liquefaction of the yeast cells due to their bursting, creates the illusion of both yeast and sugar dissolving into a liquid.

### 3. Drafting an Answer: Putting it all Together

The "disappearing yeast" experiment showcases the fascinating interplay between osmosis, biochemical reactions, and the unique properties of living cells. While the initial ingredients appear solid, the interaction between yeast and sugar triggers a series of events that result in a liquid product. This transformation highlights the power of microscopic processes and the intricate workings of biological systems.

**Additional Points:**

- The "liquid" formed is not a true solution as it contains suspended particles and dissolved compounds.
- The experiment demonstrates the importance of water in biological processes and its role in facilitating chemical reactions.
- The "disappearing yeast" serves as a simple yet effective illustration of the complex relationship between living organisms and their environment.

**Please note:** This answer is based on my current knowledge and understanding. It is always advisable to consult reliable sources for further information and scientific verification.

$\begingroup$

The whole process is called [ osmosis ](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osmosis)
. In it there is the flow of liquid along a concentration gradient. Water then
flows from the side which contains the low concentration of dissolved
molecules (this can be salts or sugar for example) to the side with the higher
concentration until it reached equilibrium. This principle is shown in the
image below (all images from the Wikipeadia article on [ osmosis
](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osmosis) ):

![enter image description here](https://i.sstatic.net/S9abq.jpg)

The blue dots are the dissolved material, the concentration is high on the
right side and lower on the left. Through the dotted line in the middle (which
is a semi-permeable membrane) only the solvent can pass to reach a
concentration equilibrium. There is a pretty cool osmotic pressure simulator
available on [ Molecular Logic
](http://molo.concord.org/database/activities/72.html) which can also help
understanding the principle.

And this is exactly what happens to the yeast cells. The sugar crystalls get
dissolved (at least partly) by some of the humidity from the yeast block (this
will not work with dried yeast) and form a highly concentrated sugar solution
(also called hypertonic). The sugar concentration inside the cells is
relatively low (called hypotonic). This leads to the effort to balance the
concentration inside the cell and outside of it which then leads to a massive
efflux of water from the cells. This goes so far, that the cell membranes
break and the interior of the cells is released (nucleus, DNA, proteins and so
on) and the sugar is completely dissolved in the released water. The reason
why this mixture is so "gooey" afterwards is the DNA, which forms long, thick
strains.

![enter image description here](https://i.sstatic.net/gv3Y7.png)

This method can be used in the lab to break up cells relatively gently without
applying too much force.

When baking you should make sure, that your yeast is not coming directly into
contact with undissolved sugar (or salt which works the same way), as this
will kill a part of your yeast cells. However, for baking you usually dissolve
the yeast in water or milk, so there is a huge excess of water which dissolves
the sugar (or salt) and protects the cells. Addionally your yeast is much
better distributed in the dough and gives better results.
